clue.text: Some nonsense about racket that's carved up fertile ground

indicators.note: about means around, so the nonsense word is placed around the rearranged racket

parts.note: blah is a bit of meaningless talk, some nonsense

indicators.note: something carved up is cut into pieces and redistributed, so the letters of racket are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as part of the fodder

explanation.surface: A complaint that some silly talk about a noisy racket led to farmland being divided up.
explanation.walkthrough: RACKET 'that's carved up' becomes CKEART, and BLAH goes 'about' it, split as BLA and H. Black earth is the rich dark soil of the steppes, also called chernozem.
explanation.definitionFit: Black earth is a very rich dark soil, prized by farmers as among the most productive land anywhere.

clue.text: Macho guy promises on paper to be intellectual?

parts.note: a stud is a man who thinks himself irresistible
an IOU is a scribbled promise to pay, and here there are several

explanation.surface: A swaggering ladies' man whose written promises to pay hint at a bookish side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Promises' reads as a verb with the macho guy as its subject; it is a plural noun. IOUs are the standard way a setter buys the letters I, O and U.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone studious is given over to books and study, which is the adjective 'intellectual' applied to a person.

clue.text: Detective receiving cut, having secured second data storage item

indicators.note: To secure something is to hold it fast inside you, so what is named next is kept within these letters.

parts.note: a dick is a detective in old crime slang, and the cut takes its last letter
s = second, the letter written after a count of them

explanation.surface: A detective on the take, pocketing his share after coming second in something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dick' for a detective is Chandler-era slang and still crossword currency. 'Cut' is the shortening here rather than a share of the money the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc is the round object data is written on to — a CD, or the platter spinning inside a hard drive.

clue.text: Swiftness shown by father, out of delicacy

indicators.note: Taking one thing out of another leaves only what was not taken, so the priest's two letters go and the rest stands.

parts.note: fragility is delicacy, and it is the word those two letters come out of
Fr is how a priest signs himself, short for Father

explanation.surface: A father moving quickly so as not to cause anyone embarrassment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of delicacy' reads as 'from tact' and is really an instruction to take letters away. Fr is the title printed in front of a Catholic priest's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Agility is quickness and lightness in moving, which is the noun 'swiftness' names.

clue.text: Ready with odd book about origin of computer navigational aid

indicators.note: about means surrounding here, so the money, odd and book letters are placed around the computer's first letter
with joins the word for odd onto the money word

parts.note: the ready is slang for cash, and so is bread
rum is an old-fashioned word for odd or strange

indicators.note: the origin of a word is where it starts, its first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A tech-sounding description of a strange manual about the beginnings of computing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is a noun here: 'the ready' is British slang for money. BREAD, RUM and B go 'about' C, the 'origin of computer'. On a website a breadcrumb trail shows where you are, as in Hansel and Gretel.
explanation.definitionFit: Breadcrumb links on a website show the path back through pages, an aid to finding your way around.

clue.text: Spot that woman's instrument

parts.note: a zit is a pimple, a spot on the skin
her is the possessive of 'that woman', as in that woman's coat

explanation.surface: Noticing the musical instrument a woman across the room is holding.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to point something out; 'spot' is the blemish instead. A zither is the flat stringed box played on a table, famous for the Third Man theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A zither is a stringed instrument, its strings stretched across a shallow soundbox and plucked, so the plain word covers it.

clue.text: Prominent figure elevating new energy source

indicators.note: To elevate is to carry upwards, and in a down clue letters carried upwards are read from the bottom of the column.

parts.note: n = new, the dictionary's short form
oil is an energy source, running up the column

explanation.surface: A famous name lending weight to a new source of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elevating' works only because this is a down entry; the same three words across would need a different instruction. N for 'new' is one of the single letters worth learning cold.
explanation.definitionFit: A lion is a person of great note — a literary lion, a lion of the bar — which is the prominent-figure sense.

clue.text: Heavy shoe enclosing sheer garments

definitions.note: Garments is plural and clothing is a mass noun, but the two swap freely: a shop selling garments sells clothing.

indicators.note: To enclose a thing is to shut it in on every side, so the shoe's letters close round what follows.

parts.note: a clog is the wooden-soled shoe of the northern mill towns
sheer fabric is thin enough to see through

explanation.surface: A clumsy wooden shoe with something flimsy stuffed inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheer' has several senses — utter, steep, vertical — and the fabric one is wanted. Clogs were the working footwear of the Lancashire mills, which is what makes them heavy.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing is the collective word for the things people wear, which is what a pile of garments amounts to.

clue.text: Dried food is submerged in water

indicators.note: Something submerged in water has the water closing over it on every side, so one word sits inside the other.

parts.note: rain is water, and it parts in the middle
the word is used just as it stands

explanation.surface: A piece of dried food lying at the bottom of a glass of water.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a plain statement of fact, and that is the disguise: 'is' is not the verb joining two halves but two letters of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A raisin is a grape dried in the sun and eaten as it is, so 'dried food' names it squarely.

clue.text: One repeatedly interrupts Australian band, generating sharp response?

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into, so the letters for one go inside the band's name, each at its own break

parts.note: AC/DC is the famous Australian hard-rock band
I is the Roman numeral for one
repeatedly supplies the one a second time, another I

explanation.surface: Someone keeps barging in on a rock band's gig, provoking a sharp reaction.
explanation.walkthrough: I 'interrupts' ACDC once, making ACDIC, and 'repeatedly' adds a second I after the first C.
explanation.definitionFit: An acidic substance produces a sour, sharp taste on the tongue; the question mark marks the loose descriptive definition.

clue.text: Disliking Liberal's pledge in Government

parts.note: l = Liberal, the party letter beside a candidate's name
an oath is a solemn pledge
the word is used just as it stands
g = Government, the Whitehall short form

explanation.surface: A promise a Liberal made once his party was inside the Government.
explanation.walkthrough: Two of the four pieces are single letters off the political page, L for Liberal and G for Government. 'In' is simply itself, which is the easiest word in any clue to overlook.
explanation.definitionFit: To be loathing something is to be disliking it with disgust — the same act, several degrees stronger.

clue.text: Scoundrel, after a lot of funny stuff, returned in charge of a sort of Government

indicators.note: What comes after something stands behind it, so in an across entry the scoundrel's letters follow the ones he is put after.
A lot of a thing is most of it and not all, so the word turns up without its final letter.
Something returned comes back the way it went, so those letters are read from the end.

parts.note: i/c is in charge, as in the officer i/c stores
a rat is a scoundrel, the sort who betrays his friends
funny stuff is COMEDY, most of which is COMED, written back to front

explanation.surface: A villain back from a comedy turn and now running some kind of government.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Scoundrel' is the only sign it belongs behind the rest rather than in front of it. 'In charge' is i/c, two letters off an army noticeboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Democratic describes whatever belongs to a democracy, which is one sort of government among monarchies and dictatorships.

clue.text: Broadcast their carol, requiring no response?

indicators.note: To broadcast seed is to fling it wide across a field, so the letters land in no particular order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: Someone's Christmas carol being put out on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is the farming sense, seed scattered by hand, rather than anything to do with radio. The question mark marks the definition as a description of a question rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhetorical question is asked for effect with no answer expected, so it is precisely one requiring no response.

clue.text: Stack building items, removing first and last

indicators.note: the opening and closing letters of the word for building items are taken off

parts.note: bricks are the items a builder uses for walls

explanation.surface: A builder piles up materials, then takes the end ones away.
explanation.walkthrough: BRICKS loses its 'first and last' letters. A rick is a stack of hay or straw.
explanation.definitionFit: A rick is a large stack of hay, corn or straw, often thatched to keep out the rain.

clue.text: Chapter not so much about French writer's skill

parts.note: c = chapter, the short form used in citations

indicators.note: A book written about a man goes all round its subject, so these letters close over the name that follows.

parts.note: less means not so much, and the word parts after its first two letters
Jules Verne, who wrote Around the World in Eighty Days

explanation.surface: A chapter that turns out not to be about a French novelist's craft after all.
explanation.walkthrough: Verne is the French writer setters reach for when they need those five letters. 'Not so much' is a comparative phrase pressed into service as a single word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleverness is the knack of doing a thing well and ingeniously, the sense of skill that praises the trick rather than the training.

clue.text: Exhausted soils within forest, say, providing shock

indicators.note: within means inside, so the emptied word goes into the trees

parts.note: a forest is an example of trees, hence the 'say'

indicators.note: exhausted means emptied, so the inside of soils is cleared, leaving its outer letters

parts.note: the word whose first and last letters remain

explanation.surface: Worn-out ground in a woodland gives someone a nasty jolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shock' wants to mean a fright, but it is a shock of hair. Emptied soils leaves SS, which goes 'within' TREES.
explanation.definitionFit: A shock is a thick mass of hair, and tresses are long locks of hair, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Visitor having time off — she's dodging husband's suggestions?

indicators.note: A day off is a day taken out of the week, so the letter named before it goes missing.
To dodge a thing is to keep clear of it altogether, so that letter never appears.

parts.note: a guest is a visitor
t = time, the letter taken off
she's, the two words run together
h = husband, as on a form

explanation.surface: A visitor with an afternoon free, keeping out of the husband's way.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves lose one letter to a standard abbreviation, t for time and h for husband, and spotting the second is the work. The dash is punctuation, not instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A guess is a suggestion put forward without certainty, which is why the question mark softens the definition.

clue.text: Mostly cancel insignificant investigation

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter of the word for cancel is dropped

parts.note: to scrub a plan is to cancel it
tiny means very small, insignificant

explanation.surface: Someone advises scrapping most of a minor inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' cuts SCRUB to SCRU, and TINY follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrutiny is close, careful examination, so it is a kind of investigation.

clue.text: US city's year satisfactory with Republican brought in after big city upset

indicators.note: after places the year-and-okay part following the reversed city
upset means turned over, so the word for big city is read backwards in this down clue

parts.note: the Great Wen is an old nickname for London, so a wen is a big city in crosswords

indicators.note: brought in means taken inside, so the Republican letter goes into the year and okay letters

parts.note: OK means satisfactory or acceptable

explanation.surface: A note on a US city's year going well, with a Republican elected after a big-city shock.
explanation.walkthrough: WEN, Cobbett's name for sprawling London, is 'upset' to NEW. R is 'brought in' to Y OK, giving YORK, placed 'after' it.
explanation.definitionFit: New York is the most populous city in the United States, so it is a US city by example.

clue.text: Soccer team backed bringing in that chap, top man in hot surroundings?

indicators.note: bringing in means taking something inside, so the pronoun goes between the reversed team letters
backed means turned back, so the team's letters are read in reverse

parts.note: FC stands for Football Club, the usual tag on a soccer team's name
he is the pronoun for that chap

explanation.surface: A football club in retreat takes on a man who could lead in a heated situation.
explanation.walkthrough: FC is 'backed' to CF, then HE goes in. A head cook is the top man in the heat of a kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A chef is the head cook, the boss of a kitchen, which is a famously hot place to work.

clue.text: French boyfriend engaged in surreptitious relations

indicators.note: To be engaged in something is to be caught up inside it, so these letters sit within the others.

parts.note: fly is British slang for sly and knowing, as in a fly one
a Frenchwoman's boyfriend is her ami, the French for friend

explanation.surface: A French boyfriend caught up in a secret affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' meaning sly is the British sense — a fly customer is one you cannot catch out. 'Relations' is the blood sense, not the affair the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: Relations, in the plural, are the people you are related to — aunts, cousins, in-laws — which is a family.

clue.text: Finished refrain in swamp

parts.note: when a thing is over it is finished
the burden of a song is its refrain, the line that comes round again

explanation.surface: The last chorus of a song dying away out on the marshes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burden' for the refrain of a song is the old sense, kept alive by setters long after singers dropped it. 'Swamp' is the verb, to overwhelm, not the marsh the surface paints.
explanation.definitionFit: To overburden someone is to load them with more than they can carry, which is what swamping a person with work does.

clue.text: Following Frenchmen in France he gets covered in earth with a sticky feel

indicators.note: What follows something comes along behind it, so the French word is written after the two Frenchmen.

parts.note: clay is earth, and it splits after its first three letters

indicators.note: Being covered in earth leaves it all round you, so those letters close over what they cover.

parts.note: MM is the French plural of M for Monsieur, used for two or more men
il is 'he' in French

explanation.surface: A man in France ending up caked in wet soil behind two other Frenchmen.
explanation.walkthrough: The French comes twice over: MM for a pair of Monsieurs, il for 'he'. The answer is an adverb, which is why the definition has to be a phrase starting 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done clammily is done with the cold damp stickiness of a nervous handshake, which is the sticky feel meant.

clue.text: Hopeless, after Bishop released stuff not meant for release?

indicators.note: Letting a thing go releases it, and a letter released from a word is simply gone from it.

parts.note: a bleak outlook is a hopeless one
B is the bishop on a chess scoresheet

explanation.surface: A bishop, once let out, handing round papers nobody meant to publish.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that the definition describes the thing rather than translating it — the material, not the act. B for bishop comes off the chessboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A leak is the confidential material that reaches the press by a back door, which is exactly what was never meant to be released.

clue.text: Surprised comment about world leader yielding power in rebellion

indicators.note: A remark made about someone goes round its subject, so these letters close over the name.

parts.note: 'my!' is the surprised comment, and it parts to take the rest

indicators.note: To yield a thing is to give it up, so that letter is surrendered and never written.

parts.note: Vladimir Putin, the Russian president
p = power, the letter given up

explanation.surface: An astonished remark about a head of state surrendering power during an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yielding power' is the joke: a president who gives up nothing but the letter p. 'My!' is a small exclamation setters lean on whenever they need those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutiny is a rising by crew or soldiers against the officers over them, which is a rebellion.

clue.text: Mark has excellent staff

parts.note: M was the mark, Germany's currency before the euro
ace means excellent, first-rate

explanation.surface: A man called Mark who employs first-rate people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like employees and is the pole: the one carried before the Speaker in the Commons, without which the House cannot sit. Mark is the German coin, not the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A mace is the ornamental staff carried before a mayor or a Speaker as the emblem of their authority.

clue.text: Flower trouble kept returning

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the trouble and kept words are read backwards together

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict
had means kept or held

explanation.surface: A flower caused bother that kept coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: AIL and HAD together, 'returning', read DAH LIA.
explanation.definitionFit: The dahlia is a showy garden plant with large blooms, named after the botanist Anders Dahl.

clue.text: Depth? Start to relish one board game involving knight

indicators.note: To involve someone is to draw them into the middle of the business, so these letters close round the next one.
Where a word starts is its opening letter, so only the first letter of what follows is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of RELISH
the Roman numeral for one
chess is the board game, and it opens after its first two letters
N is the knight in chess notation, since K is taken by the king

explanation.surface: Starting to enjoy a board game in which a knight is causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The knight is N because the king has already claimed K, a chess convention worth owning outright. The game in the wordplay is the same one the knight came from, which is how the surface holds together.
explanation.definitionFit: Richness is depth in the sense a flavour or a colour has it, the quality of having a great deal packed in.
